items.key: ai:is the 6pm eating rule a total myth? nutritionist reveals the truth about late-night dinners and weight loss
items.text: Is the 6pm eating rule a total myth? Nutritionist reveals the truth about late-night dinners and weight loss
items.article: Nutrition expert Emma Bardwell insists that this on-trend belief deserves a reality check. The clock strikes six, and across the UK a huge swathe of dieters mentally step away from the fridge. It’s a rule ingrained in many people as the ultimate sin – eating after 6pm has achieved as much notoriety as a bag full of biscuits when it comes to causing weight gain. Intermittent fasting is championed by celebs and scientists alike and usually involves setting an early cut-off time for food, putting late-night snacking firmly on the weight-gain hit list. Imposing rigid eating windows to aid weight loss has led hopeful dieters to believe that any morsel swallowed after sunset goes straight to their waistlines. However, nutrition expert Emma Bardwell insists that this on-trend belief deserves a reality check. Nutritionist Emma Bardwell says that eating after 6pm doesn't stop you losing weight. 'The idea that eating after 6pm automatically makes you gain weight is far too simplistic,' Emma says. 'Your body doesn’t suddenly start storing everything you eat as fat when the clock strikes six. For weight gain, the biggest factor is still your overall energy balance. If you regularly consume more energy – calories - than your body uses, you’re likely to gain weight, whether those excess calories are eaten at 11am or 9pm. Equally, you can eat dinner after 6pm every night and still lose weight if you’re consistently in an energy deficit.'

items.article: Frome, Somerset: With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the trees Frome, Somerset: With a sway and a swoosh, we’re entering the season to enjoy psithurism – the aural quality of the breeze in the trees T he wind-catchers along the bottom of the valley miss nothing. Even the lightest breath has them whispering. And when the wind strengthens, they do a good imitation of the river streaming over boulders below their feet. Truly, when it blows, it pours. Pass a poplar and you are enjoying the best example of psithurism, the sound of wind in trees. All this growing season, I have listened politely to oaks, alders and willows, but if I rocked up in a pub looking for chatty company, I’d want a poplar on the bar stool next to me. The name psithurism seems to have been conjured up from Greek roots as recently as the 19th century, yet the practice is as old as humanity. It exposes a curious and inescapable fact – wind itself has no voice. The explorer‑conservationist John Muir tramped many a mile through America’s wild lands, observing that “winds are advertisements of what they touch”. He may well have been thinking of talkative, animated aspens, but all members of the poplar clan are physiologically equipped to shoot the breeze with a wide range of sound and movement. items.article: Superfan and journalist Michael Cragg uncovers the Kylie behind the glitter Published: 18:00, 24 September 2026 | Updated: 18:00, 24 September 2026 As chat-up lines go, it was crude. The first time bad-boy rock star Michael Hutchence clapped eyes on good-girl pop star Kylie Minogue , it was at an Australian Music Awards after-party in 1987. The charismatic INXS frontman slurred drunkenly, ‘I don’t know what we should do first – have lunch or have sex.’ Then, before she could reply, he vanished into the night. Kylie Minogue with then boyfriend Michael Hutchence A couple of years later, his approach was more sophisticated. The story goes that Hutchence seduced his fellow Australian by reading aloud to her from Milan Kundera’s philosophical novel Immortality. Years later, Kylie still named it as her favourite book of all time. One of the things she liked about it, she explained, was its presentation of fame as a masochistic pursuit, because your reward for successfully running it to ground is invariably to become the quarry. ‘You are a winner, but you are a loser,’ was the way she put it.

items.article: A rare 1,700-year-old fragment of Homer's Odyssey has been found tucked between the pages of a Dutch library book. By XANTHA LEATHAM, EXECUTIVE SCIENCE EDITOR Published: 10:55, 17 September 2026 | Updated: 10:55, 17 September 2026 A rare 1,700–year–old fragment of Homer's Odyssey has been found tucked between the pages of a Dutch library book. A researcher was looking through a collection of old Egyptian texts at Utrecht University Library when he came across a torn piece of parchment. Closer inspection revealed the fragment, which measures just 2.6 by 3 inches (6.6 by 7.7cm), includes verses from Book 12 of the epic Greek poem. It describes what happened when Odysseus's crew ate the immortal cattle of the sun god Helios – despite his express prohibition.

items.text: I was clinging to life after my appendix burst. Then Jesus walked into the operating room... he looked nothing like I was taught
items.article: A construction worker says he had a three-hour conversation with Jesus and vividly remembers his face in an experience that changed the course of his life. By CHRIS MELORE, US DEPUTY SCIENCE EDITOR Published: 16:00, 12 September 2026 | Updated: 05:54, 13 September 2026 A construction worker in Tennessee says he came face-to-face with Jesus when he nearly died and is now sharing exactly what he looked like. Mike McKinsey was a superintendent in 2004 when he suffered a ruptured appendix that nearly killed him and required emergency surgery due to the severe infection. As his life hung in the balance, McKinsey claimed that Jesus walked into the operating room in physical form and took his hand, transporting the dying man to a hill overlooking what he perceived as heaven. Unlike other depictions across Christianity, McKinsey said he vividly remembered Jesus having darker skin, green or blue-green eyes and shoulder-length, wavy brown hair.

items.text: New 'code' found in Egypt's Great Pyramid may finally reveal its true purpose
items.article: The Great Pyramid has guarded its secrets behind millions of tons of stone, but a new paper claims its greatest message may have been hiding in plain sight. By STACY LIBERATORE, US SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR Published: 20:45, 10 September 2026 | Updated: 19:33, 11 September 2026 Independent researcher Sefy Levy argued that carefully chosen measurements on the monument’s exterior form a numerical system designed to survive long after its builders were gone. Rather than being carved into a wall , the alleged code is said to be embedded in the pyramid’s height, base, sloping sides and overall shape. Levy claimed those dimensions produce striking matches with the cycles of the moon, the calendar and planets visible to the naked eye. He believes the numbers were intended to preserve the Egyptians’ knowledge of mathematics, time and the heavens for eternity.
